title: What Happens When You Buy a Stock? (Not What You Think)
description:
When you buy a share, your money almost never goes to the company. Your broker routes the order to an exchange or a market maker, it's matched with a seller, and one business day later (T+1, the US rule since May 28, 2024) the cash and shares swap hands.

Sources: SEC press release 2024-62 on the T+1 settlement cycle (compliance date May 28, 2024); Apple Inc. Form 10-K for fiscal 2026 (14,532,182,000 shares outstanding as of Oct 23, 2026). Apple is used only as a size example, not a recommendation. Not financial advice.

#stockmarket #investing #howstockswork #financialliteracy #personalfinance

scenes.say: When you buy a share, your money almost never goes to the company.
It goes to another investor who's selling. The company only got money when it first sold those shares.
Your app is a broker. It sends the order to an exchange, or to a market maker, a firm that trades all day. A seller is matched almost instantly.
But it isn't final yet. US trades settle one business day later. That's called T plus one, the rule since May twenty twenty-four. It used to be two days.

visual.sub: one business day · was T+2 · source: SEC

scenes.say: On settlement day, a clearinghouse swaps the cash and shares. The seller gets your money. You get the share.
What do you own? A tiny slice of a real business. One Apple share is about one in fourteen and a half billion.
